title: air brake adjustment
objectives: Explain why air brake adjustment must be checked regularly and who is responsible for it
State the maximum pushrod travel limits for the applied stroke and pry (free stroke) methods
Explain how to measure air brake chamber pushrod travel and adjust a manual slack adjuster
Identify common misconceptions about air brake adjustment and the facts that correct them

sections.title: Why adjustment is critical — and the law
points: Foundation brakes are the most important part of any braking system; poor adjustment defeats even the best air system.
Brake failures and runaways are almost never caused by air system failure — poor maintenance and missed daily checks are.
Daily pre- and post-trip inspections, including checking and adjusting brakes, are mandatory.
Federal and provincial laws require daily checks of manual and automatic slack adjusters during the pre-trip inspection.
You must also check brakes before driving down steep grades posted with regulatory signs.
The driver is ultimately responsible for brake condition, even if the company has a maintenance crew.
mustKnow: You may be fined as much as $2,000 if you're operating a vehicle with brakes that are defective, including excessive brake chamber pushrod stroke.
Check air brake chamber pushrod travel at least daily.
The driver may be held responsible if the brakes are incorrectly adjusted or not working properly.

check.q: Who is ultimately responsible for ensuring the brakes are operating properly before a vehicle is moved?
check.explanation: One person is ultimately responsible for the brakes before the vehicle is moved — the driver.

check.q: What is the maximum fine for operating a vehicle with defective brakes, including excessive pushrod stroke?
check.explanation: The manual states you may be fined as much as $2,000 for operating with defective brakes.

sections.title: How s-cam adjustment works — released, applied, hot and cold drums
points: Pushrod travel is the distance the pushrod extends from the air brake chamber when brakes are applied.
The common Type 30 chamber has a maximum available stroke of 2½ inches (65 mm); the Type 30LS has three inches.
A correctly adjusted brake strokes less than half its maximum when applied.
When correctly adjusted, running clearance between lining and drum is only a few thousandths of an inch.
An out-of-adjustment brake may still seem effective while the drum is cool — a false sense of security.
Hot cast iron drums expand, making the chamber stroke further; a sudden stop could bottom out the chamber.
On long downgrades, hot drum expansion can cause total loss of braking and a runaway.
mustKnow: Type 30 chambers have a maximum available stroke of 2½ inches (65 mm); a Type 30LS has a maximum available stroke of three inches.
Each brake on an axle should be adjusted to have a similar amount of pushrod travel to the brake on the other side.
Cast iron brake drums expand when heated, causing the air chamber to stroke further as the temperature rises.

check.q: What is the maximum available stroke of a standard Type 30 air brake chamber?
check.explanation: The Type 30, the most common chamber on trucks and trailers, has a maximum available stroke of 2½ inches (65 mm).

check.q: Why can an incorrectly adjusted brake fail on a long downgrade even though it worked when cold?
choices: Hot drums expand and the chamber can bottom out
check.explanation: Heated cast iron drums expand, increasing stroke until the chamber bottoms out and braking power is lost.

sections.title: Checking adjustment — applied stroke, pry method, indicators and limits
points: Before checking, park safely, block the wheels, build full air pressure, release spring parking brakes, and shut the engine off.
Applied stroke method: mark the pushrod at rest, then hold a full 90 to 100 p.s.i. application and measure the difference.
The applied stroke method is used by roadside inspectors and usually needs two people.
Pry method: push the pushrod fully in, mark it, pry it out with a bar, and measure free stroke.
New pushrods have a marking (usually red) that shows when adjustment is needed immediately — don't wait for it to appear.
Adjust before your measurements approach the maximum limits — they are maximums, not targets.
mustKnow: Applied stroke: 1 inch to 1½ inches (25 to 38 mm) is a good range; more than 1¾ of an inch (45 mm) means the brakes need adjustment.
Free stroke (pry method): ½ to ¾ of an inch (12 to 20 mm) is a good range; more than ¾ of an inch (20 mm) means the brakes need adjustment.
Apply and hold a full brake application of 90 to 100 p.s.i. (620 – 690 kPa) for the applied stroke method.
Reservoir pressure must be at least 100 p.s.i. (690 kPa) before checking, with parking brakes released.
If the red marking on the pushrod is visible at the chamber face, the brake is dangerously out of adjustment and needs immediate attention.

check.q: Using the applied stroke method on a Type 30 chamber with a manual slack adjuster, brakes need adjustment when travel exceeds:
check.explanation: More than 1¾ of an inch (45 mm) of applied stroke means the brakes need adjustment.

check.q: Using the pry method, brakes need adjustment when free stroke is more than:
check.explanation: Free stroke of more than ¾ of an inch (20 mm) means the brakes need adjustment.

sections.title: Manual vs automatic slack adjusters — and misconceptions
points: To adjust a manual slack adjuster, depress the locking sleeve and turn the adjusting bolt with a 9/16 inch wrench.
Correct direction: the cam rotates as if the brakes were applying; the pushrod must never move in or out.
Turn until solid resistance (lining contacts drum), then back off about 1/3 of a turn for running clearance.
All commercial trucks and trailers with air brakes have been built with automatic slack adjusters since 1996.
Automatic slack adjusters self-adjust in normal driving but must still be checked daily on the pre-trip inspection.
Manually adjusting automatic slack adjusters is dangerous — it gives a false sense of security and is emergency-only.
You cannot reliably check adjustment from the cab, by pressure drop, or by the 90-degree slack adjuster angle.
mustKnow: With an automatic slack adjuster on a Type 30 chamber, brakes need repair if applied stroke is more than two inches (50 mm) or free stroke is more than ¾ of an inch (20 mm).
Manufacturers recommend automatic slack adjusters be checked by a mechanic at every chassis lubrication interval, every 40,000 km, or every three months, whichever comes first.
A Transport Canada study showed vehicles with manual slack adjusters were put out-of-service at a rate 150 per cent higher than those with automatic slack adjusters.
Under B.C. Commercial Vehicle Safety and Enforcement rules, it's illegal to retrofit manual slack adjusters on a vehicle manufactured with automatic slack adjusters.
Some parking brake control valves stay open with as little as 20 p.s.i. (138 kPa), so ensure 90 to 100 p.s.i. before checking adjustment.

check.q: Since what year have all commercial trucks and trailers with air brakes been manufactured with automatic slack adjusters?
check.explanation: All air-braked commercial trucks and trailers have been built with automatic slack adjusters since 1996.

check.q: What does it usually mean if an automatic slack adjuster strokes beyond the maximum allowed?
choices: It just needs a quick manual adjustment
The brake drums are too cold
There are other brake problems needing a qualified mechanic
check.explanation: Excessive stroke usually means the adjuster failed, was installed incorrectly, or the foundation brake has a problem needing repair.

summary: The driver is legally responsible for checking brake adjustment daily — fines can reach $2,000 for defective brakes.
Manual slack adjuster limits on a Type 30: adjust if applied stroke exceeds 1¾ inch (45 mm) or free stroke exceeds ¾ inch (20 mm).
Hot brake drums expand and increase stroke — a brake that works cold can bottom out and cause a runaway.
Always block wheels, build at least 100 p.s.i., release parking brakes, and shut off the engine before checking.
Never routinely hand-adjust automatic slack adjusters — excessive stroke (over two inches applied) means repair by a qualified mechanic.
